questiontext.text: What is the defining difference between a radix tree (compressed trie) and a plain trie?

answer.text: Chains of single-child nodes are compressed, so each edge is labeled with a whole substring

feedback.text: Correct — that compression is exactly what defines a radix/Patricia tree.

answer.text: Each node has exactly three children

feedback.text: No — that describes a ternary search tree, not a radix tree.

answer.text: Keys are compared by hashing them to buckets

feedback.text: No — a radix tree still walks the key; it does not hash.

answer.text: It stores only numeric keys, never strings

feedback.text: No — radix trees handle string/byte keys just like tries.

generalfeedback.text: A radix tree is a trie in which every chain of single-child nodes is merged into one edge labeled with the whole shared substring.

questiontext.text: In a radix tree, what does a single edge carry?

answer.text: A whole substring (possibly several characters)

feedback.text: Correct — compressed edges are labeled with multi-character substrings.

answer.text: Exactly one character

feedback.text: No — that is a plain trie; the radix tree merges single-child chains.

answer.text: A less-than / equal / greater-than pointer

feedback.text: No — that is a ternary search tree node.

answer.text: A hash of the remaining key

feedback.text: No — radix trees store literal substrings on edges, not hashes.

generalfeedback.text: Because single-child chains are compressed, a radix-tree edge is labeled with the entire shared substring rather than one character.

questiontext.text: Compared with a plain trie storing the same keys, a radix tree mainly...

answer.text: Saves space by collapsing single-child chains, while keeping O(L) operations

feedback.text: Correct — fewer nodes, same O(L) time on a key of length L.

answer.text: Reduces search time from O(L) to O(log L)

feedback.text: No — operations stay O(L); the win is in space, not asymptotic time.

answer.text: Makes the structure comparison-based like a BST

feedback.text: No — it is still a trie; it navigates by characters, not comparisons.

answer.text: Loses the ability to answer prefix queries

feedback.text: No — it keeps the same prefix-query strengths as a trie.

generalfeedback.text: Compression removes redundant single-child nodes, cutting memory while search, insert, and delete of a length-L key remain O(L).

questiontext.text: Which application is a classic use of radix trees?

answer.text: IP routing tables (longest-prefix match)

feedback.text: Correct — radix/Patricia trees are a staple of IP routing.

answer.text: Balancing a set of numbers for median queries

feedback.text: No — that is order-statistic territory, not radix trees.

answer.text: Priority-queue scheduling by key value

feedback.text: No — that is a heap's job, not a radix tree's.

answer.text: Cache eviction with least-recently-used order

feedback.text: No — LRU uses a list plus map, not a radix tree.

generalfeedback.text: Radix (Patricia) trees are widely used for IP routing tables and similar prefix-matching workloads.

questiontext.text: Compressing a trie into a radix tree keeps search, insert, and delete of a length-L key at O(L).

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — compression saves space without changing the O(L) time.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: No — operations remain O(L); only the node count shrinks.

questiontext.text: A radix tree generally uses more memory than the plain trie holding the same keys.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — compression removes single-child nodes, so it uses less memory.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — the radix tree saves space compared with a plain trie.

questiontext.text: A radix tree that compresses single-child chains is also historically known as a ______ tree (one word, the classic name).

answer.text: Patricia

feedback.text: Correct — the radix tree is also called a Patricia tree/trie.

answer.text: Patricia*

feedback.text: Correct — the radix tree is also called a Patricia tree/trie.

questiontext.text: Which statements about radix trees are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: They merge single-child chains, labeling edges with whole substrings

feedback.text: Yes — that is the compression that defines them.

answer.text: They keep the same prefix-query strengths as an ordinary trie

feedback.text: Yes — shared prefixes still lead to a common subtree.

answer.text: They are comparison-based like a balanced BST

feedback.text: No — a radix tree is still a trie, navigating by characters.

answer.text: Compression raises operation cost above O(L)

feedback.text: No — operations remain O(L).

generalfeedback.text: Radix trees compress single-child chains to save space, retain trie-style prefix queries, stay non-comparison-based, and keep O(L) operations.
